title: Concerning Liberality and Meanness
coreMove: Prefer the reproach of thrift to the public hatred produced by generosity that must be funded through extraction.
sourcePressure: The chapter follows the chain from maintaining a reputation for liberality to exhausting resources, taxing subjects, becoming rapacious, hated, poor, and unable to defend the state. Thrift can later appear useful because it funds defense and enterprises without extraordinary burdens, while generosity with other people's property works differently from squandering one's own or one's subjects' resources.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The wrong version becomes personal frugality advice or anti-charity moralizing. The writer must show the political sequence: visible liberality consumes revenue, forces taxation or robbery, creates hatred, and weakens defense.

hook: a generous CEO learning to cut perks
counterintuition: most people assume generosity is good, but actually thrift wins
tryThisNow: set a timer for ninety seconds and list expenses to cut

exampleSpecs.domain: a mountain prince canceling victory games after seeing the winter pass repair estimate
exampleSpecs.audience: a ruler tempted to keep the name of openhanded victor with public games
exampleSpecs.stakes: the games win praise from a few now, but the pass wall will fail unless repairs are funded without a new hearth tax
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: He sets the gilded race wreath on top of the cracked pass-stone estimate, then signs the repair order and accepts that the poets will call him mean.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A gilded race wreath rests on a cracked pass-stone estimate.
mustAvoid: chapter 10 wall logistics as main lesson

exampleSpecs.domain: a river monarchy deciding whether to remit ferry tolls for a coronation month
exampleSpecs.audience: a new monarch whose council wants a visible gift to secure affection
exampleSpecs.stakes: remitting tolls looks liberal, but replacing the revenue with market levies would make every trader pay for a short-lived cheer
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before the herald reads the remission decree, the treasurer lays the missing toll counters beside the market levy slips and shows whose purse will supply the applause.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Missing toll counters are stacked beside blank market levy slips.

exampleSpecs.domain: a frontier army dividing captured enemy stores instead of the home treasury before a long campaign
exampleSpecs.audience: a commander deciding when liberality with others' goods is politically different
exampleSpecs.stakes: soldiers must be followed in the field, but spending the home treasury would burden subjects who are not receiving the spoils
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The commander asks which chest can be opened without taxing home villages, then breaks the enemy store seal and leaves the subject-tax coffer locked.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: An enemy store seal lies beside a locked subject-tax coffer.

exampleSpecs.domain: a harbor ruler refusing a marble quay dedication while building patrol boats from saved customs revenue
exampleSpecs.audience: councillors embarrassed that visiting envoys will see a plain quay
exampleSpecs.stakes: marble creates a reputation for magnificence, but patrol boats prevent raiders without imposing an emergency customs surcharge
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: She runs her hand over the uncarved quay block, then stamps the saved customs ledger for three patrol hulls instead of one dedication inscription.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: An uncarved quay block sits beside a saved customs ledger.

exampleSpecs.domain: a desert ruler rejecting a court gift cycle that would force new well fees on caravan villages
exampleSpecs.audience: a prince whose nobles expect robes, horses, and jeweled cups every season
exampleSpecs.stakes: gifts satisfy a narrow court while well fees make distant villages hate a ruler they rarely see
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: When the steward reads the gift list, the prince places a well-fee tablet over the jeweled cup inventory and asks which names will remember the cost.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A well-fee tablet covers the corner of a jeweled cup inventory.

exampleSpecs.domain: a war widow regent ending public bread spectacles to keep the armoury supplied without confiscations
exampleSpecs.audience: a regent accused of meanness by city crowds after the funeral year
exampleSpecs.stakes: spectacle bread would preserve affection briefly, but empty armouries would invite attack and later force seizures from the same households
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The regent closes the painted bread booth, opens the armoury nail tally, and points to the confiscation order she will not have to issue if thrift holds.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A painted bread booth shutter leans against an armoury nail tally.

skillTargets: trace the chain from visible liberality to taxation, rapacity, hatred, poverty, and military weakness
distinguish spending one's own or subjects' resources from distributing goods taken in campaign
apply the difference between reproach without hatred and rapacity with hatred
evaluate whether a generous act is politically sustainable or merely reputation maintenance

tryThisNowSpec: Pick one public act of generosity by a ruler or institution. Write who visibly receives it, whose resources quietly pay for it, and whether the payment route creates reproach, hatred, or defensible thrift.
